title: Bring It to Life
tagline: Your character stops sitting there and starts moving on its own.
builtOn: Lesson 2 — your `MyCharacter` class. Keep that tab exactly as it is.
goals: Use `setVelocity(vx, vy)` to give your character a speed and a direction
Call `move()` every frame to animate it
Explain what screen wrapping is and when it happens
Use `random()` to make things different every time you run

vocab.def: how fast something moves and which way. It has two parts: left/right (`vx`) and up/down (`vy`)
one single picture in the animation. `draw()` produces one frame per tick, about 60 every second
picks a surprise number between `a` and `b`, fresh every time it is called
when a sprite goes off one edge of the screen and reappears on the opposite edge

warmup: Where does your character get drawn on the screen? Which function draws it, and how many times per second does that happen?

howItWorks.h: Velocity is two numbers, not one
p: "Speed" in a game is really two separate questions: how fast am I going sideways, and how fast am I going up or down? So velocity is two numbers.
bullets: `vx` is left and right. **Positive** goes right →. **Negative** goes left ←.
`vy` is up and down. **Positive** goes DOWN ↓. **Negative** goes UP ↑.

howItWorks.h: Yes, positive y really is down
p: This trips up almost everyone. On a math graph, y goes up. On a screen, y goes **down** — `y = 0` is the top edge, and bigger y means further down.
So `setVelocity(3, -2)` means: 3 pixels right and 2 pixels **up**, every frame.
Setting a velocity is like telling someone how fast to walk. Until they actually take a step, nothing happens.
`move()` is the step. It takes the velocity and adds it to the position, once. So it has to be inside `draw()`, where it happens 60 times a second.

code.label: The order that matters

p: If you draw before you move, you are drawing your character where it *used to be*. It is off by one frame, forever. It is a small bug and mostly harmless, but it is a good habit to get right: **move, then draw**.
Run it and wait. When your character slides off the right edge, it comes back in on the left. Off the top, back in at the bottom.
You did not write that. The library does it for you inside `move()`. That is the "magic toolbox" idea — you push the button, the button works.
`random(-5, 5)` picks a new number between -5 and 5 each time it runs. Put it where a velocity number goes and your character takes off in a different direction every single time you press Run.

steps: Open your Lesson 2 sketch. **Keep the `MyCharacter` tab exactly as it is** — you are only changing the main tab.
In `setup()`, after you create the player, add: `player.setVelocity(3, -2);`
Press **▶ Run**. Nothing moves. That is expected — you told it a speed but never told it to take a step.
Run again. Your character should drift up and to the right. Watch what happens when it reaches an edge.
Change the velocity to `(8, 0)`. Run. Now `(0.5, 0)`. Run. Fast and slow.
Try exact diagonal: `(3, 3)`. Then try `(3, -3)`. Which way does each one go?
Replace both numbers with `random(-5, 5)` and press Run five times in a row. Different every time.
Change the background color to set a mood for your character's world.

code.label: Main sketch tab (MyCharacter.pde is unchanged from Lesson 2)

makeItYours: Try `random(-5, 5)` for both velocity values in `setup()`, then run it several times.
Make your character move **really** fast. Then really slow. Which one suits it?
Make it move exactly diagonally — that means `vx` and `vy` have the same size.
Change the background color to set a mood. A drifting character on dark blue reads completely differently than on white.
Add a **second** blob with its own velocity so there is something else alive on screen.
challenge: Comment out `background(240)` and run. Your character leaves a trail, because nothing is erasing the old frames. Some of the best-looking sketches do this on purpose.
flintHint: Good things to ask: "my character will not move", "why does negative y go up?", or "how do I make it move in a random direction?" Tell it you are on Lesson 3 and paste in your `setup()` and `draw()`.
wrapup: What happens if you call `drawSprite()` before `move()`? What does that change?
assignmentTask: Give your character motion that feels like it belongs to that character.
assignmentDo: Set a velocity in `setup()` and call `move()` in `draw()`, in the right order.
Watch it wrap around the screen edges at least once.
Tune the speed until it feels right for **your** character. A heavy monster and a darting bug should not move at the same speed.
Set a background color that matches the mood.
submit: A short screen recording (a few seconds) so the motion is visible — or a screenshot plus a sentence describing how it moves.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below.
checklist: Set a velocity with two numbers (left/right, up/down).
Use `random(a, b)` to vary the motion.
standard: Use `setVelocity()` and `move()` to animate the character, with screen wrapping and `random()` for variety.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: My character is frozen. **Next step:** make sure you call `player.move()` inside `draw()`. A character with a velocity but no `move()` never budges.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: My character moves on its own and wraps around the screen edges.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and I chose a velocity that gives my character its own feel — fast, slow, diagonal, or a `random()` speed — and set a background mood to match.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I experimented with `random()` velocities across runs, or added a second self-moving blob alongside the player.

thinking: In one or two sentences: what velocity felt right for your character, and why?

di.h: Draw the axes on the board
p: Literally draw it. An arrow right labelled `+vx`, an arrow left labelled `-vx`, an arrow **down** labelled `+vy`, an arrow up labelled `-vy`.
Positive y being down surprises students every year. Getting it on the board once saves a dozen individual explanations.
Set a velocity in `setup()` and run **without** `move()`. Nothing happens. Let them sit with that for a few seconds and ask why.
Then add `move()`. The contrast makes the point better than any explanation: velocity is an intention, `move()` is the action.
`move()` first, then `drawSprite()`. If you draw first and then move, the position is one frame behind.
It is a subtle bug and mostly invisible, but naming it now builds the habit and gives you the wrap-up question.
Do **not** announce that sprites wrap. Set a velocity, run it, and let the character slide off the edge while you keep talking.
Someone will shout when it reappears on the other side. That reaction is worth more than telling them.
Put `random(-5, 5)` directly into `setVelocity()` in `setup()` and press Run four or five times in a row on the projector. Different every time.
This is also the first time they see a function call used as an argument to another function call. Do not name that. Just let it look normal.

guided: Everyone opens their Lesson 2 sketch. Confirm out loud: the `MyCharacter` tab does not change today.
Add `setVelocity(3, -2)` in `setup()` together. Run. Nothing moves. Ask why before answering.
Let it run long enough to wrap. Wait for the reaction.
As a class, try fast (`8, 0`), slow (`0.5, 0`), and diagonal (`3, 3`). Ask which direction each one goes before running it.
Swap in `random(-5, 5)` and have everyone press Run repeatedly.
Release for personalization: tune a speed that fits their character, set a background mood.
pitfalls: **Forgetting `move()`.** By far the most common. The character sits still and students assume `setVelocity` is broken.
Calling `drawSprite()` before `move()`. One-frame lag. Usually invisible, but worth a mention.
Putting `setVelocity()` inside `draw()`. It technically works, but it resets the velocity 60 times a second, which will confuse them badly in Lesson 4 when the keyboard tries to change it.
Expecting positive `vy` to go up. It goes down.

Students who drew their Lesson 2 character at **hard-coded coordinates** will see the hitbox move while the art stays put. This is where that bug surfaces. Fix: re-anchor every shape to `pos.x`/`pos.y`.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: One-frame lag — the character is drawn one step behind where it actually is. Accept any answer that gets at "it draws the old position."
notes: The hard-coded-coordinates bug from Lesson 2 becomes visible today. Expect two or three students to hit it, and treat it as a feature: it is a very clear demonstration of why the belly-button rule exists.
Wrapping is a genuine "wow" moment. Protect it by not spoiling it.
If a student asks how to make the character bounce off walls instead of wrapping, that is a great question and a great Lesson 9 extension. Park it.
Speeds above about 15 make the character hard to watch. Let them discover that rather than capping it.
